analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in December 2024, but no senator ever voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar members of Congress, and in a later version the President, Vice President, and their spouses and dependent children too, from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and (in the later version) digital assets. Anyone holding those investments would have to sell them or, in the original draft, put them in a blind trust the official cannot control, with fines for failing to comply. Diversified mutual funds, index-style ETFs, and Treasury bonds would remain allowed. The bill would also fine officials $500 for each late financial-transaction report under the existing STOCK Act and require financial disclosures to be posted online in a searchable format.
analysis.who_benefits: The public at large. Members of Congress vote on laws, subsidies, and contracts that move specific companies' stock prices; barring them and their families from holding those companies' shares removes a direct personal stake in what they legislate. Honest members who hold only diversified funds also benefit from rules that apply to everyone. The searchable disclosure database would let journalists and voters see officials' finances more easily.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens who want conflict-free lawmaking

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from buying covered investments immediately and from selling them 90 days after enactment, and requires existing holdings to be divested or placed in a qualified blind trust within 120 days, with civil penalties of at least a month's pay or 10% of the un-divested asset for noncompliance.
Excludes diversified mutual funds, diversified exchange-traded funds, and Treasury securities, so officials could still invest broadly without picking individual companies.

Requires the House and Senate ethics offices to publish certifications, trust agreements, federal payments received, and granted extensions online, and requires financial disclosures to be filed electronically in a searchable, downloadable format.
Adds a $500 fine for each failure to file a periodic transaction report required by the STOCK Act, replacing the current system where late filings carry no meaningful penalty.
The committee-approved version extended the ban to the President and Vice President and added digital assets to the list of banned investments.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President whose families hold individual stocks, commodities, or futures would have to sell those holdings within the bill's deadlines, potentially realizing taxable gains, and would lose the ability to trade during their terms. Spouses working in finance or on corporate boards would keep some exemptions but lose flexibility over household portfolios.
analysis.who_pays_short: Stock-holding federal officeholders and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts securities a spouse receives as compensation from their primary employer or from corporate board service, so a conflict of interest can survive through a spouse's own work rather than through the member's family investments.

The original version allowed compliance through qualified blind trusts, a mechanism with a long record of leaking knowledge of holdings to the beneficiary; the committee-reported version tightened this by requiring divestment and eventually phasing out blind trusts, but only starting March 31, 2027, leaving a multi-year gap.

Enforcement relies on the same ethics offices that police members today, with penalties set at roughly a month's pay or 10% of the un-divested asset per 30-day period, which for a wealthy member can be small relative to total assets.

Critics of stock-trading bans argue the rules, including limits on what a member's spouse may own, would deter wealthy people with sophisticated finances from serving in public office and raise questions about how far the government can regulate a spouse's independent career.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit, removing officials' personal stakes in the companies they regulate and legislate, is significant and the costs are real but manageable, since diversified index funds remain fully allowed. The design is not airtight: the spouse-employment carve-out leaves a channel for conflicts, the committee version does not start until March 2027, and penalties may not bite hardest against the wealthiest violators. On balance it is a serious, workable conflict-of-interest reform with some deliberate-looking exceptions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar ready for a floor vote in December 2024, but the Senate never voted on it and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on April 17, 2023 with 24 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably on July 24, 2024, and formally reported it on December 19, 2024, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

The substitute amendment expanded the ban to the President and Vice President, added digital assets, replaced the blind-trust compliance path with mandatory divestment and a phaseout of existing blind trusts, and set the main effective date at March 31, 2027.
On December 19, 2024 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 729), which made it available for a floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the Senate or the House passing the bill; all bills die when a Congress ends.
All 23 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican senator signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who own and trade individual stocks came out ahead: the rules never took effect, so they keep the ability to hold and trade individual companies' shares while voting on legislation affecting those same companies. The searchable disclosure improvements were also never enacted, leaving the status quo in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members who own and trade individual stocks

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1171 on April 17, 2023 and recruited an initial bloc of two dozen cosponsors.

for.name: 23 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed onto the bill, giving it the support needed for committee action.

for.name: Sen. Gary Peters
for.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: His committee ordered the bill reported favorably in July 2024 and formally reported it with a substitute amendment on December 19, 2024, moving it to the Senate calendar.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote, despite it sitting ready on the Senate calendar after committee approval in December 2024.

against.name: House leaders of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought any congressional stock-trading ban to the House floor during the 118th Congress, so the bill had no path even if the Senate had acted.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican senator signed on, though stock-trading bans enjoy broad public support across party lines and a version of the idea had backers in both chambers.
